title: AI scams in Georgia and South Florida: How scammers use deepfakes to steal millions

reading.body:
Criminals used generative AI to create deepfakes of voices and identities to impersonate immigration attorneys and conduct emergency scams targeting immigrants and other vulnerable populations in Georgia and South Florida. The scams involved cloning voices from social media, spoofing phone numbers, and researching victims' family relationships to make fraudulent requests appear authentic. This represents a failure of platform and communication systems to verify identity before processing financial transactions.

The deployment failure occurred at the point where money moved. Phone calls claiming to be from family members or trusted professionals reached victims with no verification mechanism in place. Banks and individuals had no automated check to confirm the caller's identity before funds were transferred. The systems accepting payments operated without requiring independent verification that the person requesting money was who they claimed to be.

It is not established whether any particular AI platform failed to implement safeguards, or whether the deepfake technology itself was deployed without safety testing. The reported losses of nearly $893 million in AI-enabled scams are based on FBI complaint data, which records victim reports rather than independently verified fraud totals.

summary:
Criminals are increasingly using artificial intelligence to commit sophisticated scams across Georgia and South Florida by creating convincing deepfakes of voices, photos, and identities. In one case, a South Florida immigration attorney discovered his voice and identity had been cloned to target vulnerable immigrants, while a Cobb County couple lost approximately $800,000 in a cryptocurrency scam. According to the FBI's 2025 Internet Crime Report, Americans reported nearly $893 million in AI-enabled scam losses last year, with Florida accounting for 350 complaints totaling $39.9 million and Georgia reporting 71 complaints worth $10.4 million in losses.

Scammers use generative AI to impersonate trusted individuals by cloning voices from social media, spoofing phone numbers, and researching victims' family relationships to make emergency requests seem authentic. The AI grandparent scam, where criminals pretend to be a relative in distress, has become particularly prevalent. Authorities recommend families create private code words to verify identities, verify urgent requests through known contact numbers, and avoid sending money based solely on phone calls. Banks urge customers to pause before responding to unexpected requests and monitor accounts closely rather than acting immediately.
